Susan Ratliff, MD, Harborlight Neurology, Portland, ME (AR)
> A generous forty minutes despite a full schedule, and most of it spent on the older half of the panel, which is a large share of this practice.
> The main hesitation with elderly patients is drug-drug interactions on top of already long medication lists.
> Explained that the pharmacy review usually happens after the visit rather than during it, so a decision often waits a week, and asked very politely whether anything shorter than the label section exists that intake staff could work from.
> I committed only to checking what may be shared and to bringing it at the next appt.

Daniel Whitcomb, MD, Northbrook Neurology Institute, Albany, NY (RSM)
> The transition-age population came up first, and without any prompting from me.
> Keeps a running list of 15- and 16-year-olds with drug-resistant focal seizures who simply have to wait until 18 before cenobamate is even an option.
> Was careful to frame this as a limit of what is approved rather than a request to work around it, and asked that the observation be carried back internally; I said I would log it as stated.
> Referrals from two regional pediatric practices have increased this year, which is part of why that list keeps growing.

Mei-Lin Tsang, MD, Bayview Epilepsy Associates, Oakland, CA (RSM)
> A short conversation in the corridor between teaching sessions, and entirely about the academic calendar.
> Two residents rotate onto the epilepsy service in October, and the fellowship journal club is moving to a Thursday evening slot so that the trainees on nights can still attend.
> Asked whether I had recieved the updated rotation schedule from the program office, which I had not; that one is on me to chase.
> No clinical or product discussion took place and nothing was requested.

Grace Lindqvist, MD, Riverstone Medical Group, Hartford, CT (RSM)
> Fifteen minutes between clinics, which the office kindly made room for at short notice.
> Asked directly whether any adolescent dosing or safety data for cenobamate is on the horizon.
> I explained that I am able to share published information within the approved adult indication for XCOPRI only, and that I would not speculate beyond it; the answer was accepted without pushback.
> Open on my side: confirm with Medical Information what may be sent, and reply before the next visit.

Fiona Gallagher, MD, Great Lakes Epilepsy Institute, Madison, WI (RSM)
> 20 min, mostly admin. Prior auth paperwork is the complaint.
> One coordinator now does appeals full time. Says the payer forms ask the same thing three diffrent ways.
> No product specifics discussed. Nothing requested.

Marcus Boudreaux, MD, Bayou Regional Epilepsy Center, Baton Rouge, LA (RSM)
> Adolescent DRE came up early, unprompted.
> Said, and I quote, 'my hardest clinic days are telling parents of a seventeen-year-old that we have nothing new to offer until adulthood.'
> Two such pts in clinic this month, both f/u in Nov.
> Framed as a label limit, not a request to go around it. Confirmed CNB is adult only, no discussion of use under 18. Logging as recurring.

Yolanda Reyes, MD, Copper Mesa Neurology, Mesa, AZ (RSM)
> Quick stop, clinic running behind. Down one MA and one front desk since Aug.
> New pt wait out to nine weeks. f/u appts get bumped first when someone calls out.
> Asked me to keep visits under 15 min until they backfill. No requests.

Peter Kowalczyk, MD, Green Mountain Neuroscience, Burlington, VT (RSM)
> Most of the appt on referral mix.
> Asked whether anyone is looking at post-stroke epilepsy, since more referrals lately are seizures after stroke.
> Stroke unit sends them straight over now, no pathway back. Guessed 5 or 6 in the last yr.
> Told them I would check what published lit exists. Promised nothing else, no product claims either side.

Jorge Maldonado, MD, Redwood Basin Medical Group, Sacramento, CA (RSM)
> End of day, 10 min. Volume up vs last quarter, mostly outside referrals.
> Two new pts a week on the epilepsy side, up from one. Says the mix is shifting older.
> Nothing clinical. Next visit Dec.

Omar Haddad, MD, Beacon Hill Epilepsy Center, Providence, RI (RSM)
> A thorough half hour, and the adolescent question arrived before I had asked anything.
> Mentioned two adolescent patients who failed carbamazepine and levetiracetam and said the treatment options in that age group feel like a dead end.
> Was explicit that this describes what is approved and available rather than a request to go beyond it; I confirmed that XCOPRI is indicated in adults only and did not discuss use below 18.
> Added that families arrive having read a good deal online and ask why the age cut-off exists at all, a conversation this clinic now has repeatedly.

Imani Okafor, MD, Smoky Ridge Medical Center, Knoxville, TN (RSM)
> The discussion stayed general and no specific agent was named at any point.
> Observed that the number of antiseizure medications in routine use at this center has grown steadily while the number of distinct mechanisms has not, and that the formulary committee now asks for class-level summaries rather than single-agent reviews.
> Asked out of curiosity how often such committees revisit a list; I did not know and did not guess.
> No comparative or efficacy claims were made by either party and no materials were requested.

Mei-Lin Tsang, MD, Bayview Epilepsy Associates, Oakland, CA (RSM)
> Brief and entirely logistical. The center plans to send three attendings and two fellows to the regional epilepsy meeting in the spring.
> Raised that the Thursday sessions collide with a full clinic day, and that travel approval at this institution now has to be filed a full quarter ahead.
> Asked whether the preliminary agenda had been circulated yet; I said I would forward it once it is public.

Katherine Ost, MD, Sonoran Neuroscience Institute, Tucson, AZ (RSM)
> A longer visit than scheduled, and the tone was noticeably positive throughout.
> Shared that two drug-resistant adults who had failed multiple ASMs are now several months with markedly fewer seizures on cenobamate.
> Was careful to add that these are two individual courses rather than a pattern anyone should read too much into, and that both patients remain under close f/u in clinic.
> No dosing specifics came up and I made no claims of my own; recording the experience only as reported.

Yolanda Reyes, MD, Copper Mesa Neurology, Mesa, AZ (RSM)
> Fifteen minutes by phone, and the subject throughout was telehealth logistics.
> Roughly half of the follow-up visits at this office are now virtual, and the no-show rate for those slots was described as lower than for in-person appts, though nobody has measured it properly.
> Two practical problems raised: patients cannot upload a seizure diary through the video platform, and interpreter scheduling still needs two days notice.
> Nothing clinical came up and no materials were requested.

Alice Nguyen-Barr, MD, Old Dominion Neurology Group, Richmond, VA (AR)
> A courtesy stop at the end of the day, and the conversation never left small talk.
> Most of it was about the storm that closed the interstate last week and a delayed flight back from a family wedding in Seattle.
> Also asked, politely, whether I ever tire of the driving between Richmond and Norfolk, which I confessed I occassionally do.
> No clinical or product discussion of any kind.

Jorge Maldonado, MD, Redwood Basin Medical Group, Sacramento, CA (RSM)
> Discussion was limited to logistics for the regional epilepsy meeting in the spring; the group plans to send two attendings and one NP this year.
> Noted that the Friday sessions overlap with a full clinic day and asked whether the agenda would be circulated in advance.
> Follow-ups: (1) forward the published agenda once available, (2) confirm whether the pre-meeting workshop requires seperate registration.

Fiona Gallagher, MD, Great Lakes Epilepsy Institute, Madison, WI (RSM)
> Most of the conversation concerned teaching load. Three residents are rotating through the epilepsy service this block, and journal club has moved to the first Tuesday of the month.
> Asked whether an MSL may sit in on journal club as an observer; I described the usual practice and said I would confirm what is permitted.
> Follow-ups: (1) confirm the observer attendance policy, (2) send the contact for room booking so the spring session can be scheduled.

Priya Raghavan, MD, North Star Neurology, Minneapolis, MN (RSM)
> Reviewed the focal-onset caseload at a high level. Most adults in the panel arrive already on one or two ASMs, referred in from primary care.
> Noted one adult on cenobamate describing daytime somnolence severe enough to affect the daily commute.
> I offered no comment on management and asked that the experience be reported through the standard safety channel; a report has been initiated on my side per procedure.
> Follow-ups: (1) provide the safety intake reference once assigned, (2) resend the patient counseling material list requested in October.

Alice Nguyen-Barr, MD, Old Dominion Neurology Group, Richmond, VA (AR)
> Conversation centered on the geriatric share of the practice, which has grown noticeably over the past two years.
> For older adults, the worry is less about efficacy and more about interaction checks and the burden of slow titration.
> Added that every new start means a separate pharmacy review and at least two additional calls to the family, absorbed by the same front-desk staff.
> Follow-ups: (1) identify which approved XCOPRI interaction reference may be shared, (2) ask Medical Information whether a caregiver-facing explainer on the titration period exists.

Yolanda Reyes, MD, Copper Mesa Neurology, Mesa, AZ (RSM)
> Short visit, mostly logistics. Down two MAs since Nov, front desk covering intake.
> New pt backlog out past ten weeks. Says f/u appt slots get eaten first when someone calls out.
> No requests this time. Keeping visits brief until staffing settles.

Mei-Lin Tsang, MD, Bayview Epilepsy Associates, Oakland, CA (RSM)
> Vented about the EHR seizure diary template. Free text only, no count feild, so frequency ends up buried in the narrative.
> Says any chart review means reading every note line by line. Wants structured fields, IT queue is long.
> Nothing to action. Logged for context only.

Katherine Ost, MD, Sonoran Neuroscience Institute, Tucson, AZ (RSM)
> Met in hallway, clinic building half under construction. Neuro clinic on second floor thru March.
> Main complaint was parking - staff lot closed, shuttle runs late. Told me to allow extra time next visit.
> No clinical discussion.

Renee Calloway, MD, Palmetto Neurology Associates, Charleston, SC (RSM)
> Longer than planned. Topic was the adolescent handoff into adult neuro.
> Estimated three or four teens in the panel each year hit the same wall: two failed ASMs, still seizing, and no access to cenobamate until age 18.
> Says families ask what changes at 18 and there is no good answer. I confirmed CNB label is adult only, did not discuss use below 18.
> Flagging as recurring unmet need. Second time from this clinic.

Fiona Gallagher, MD, Great Lakes Epilepsy Institute, Madison, WI (RSM)
> Quick check-in end of day. Volume up over last quarter, mostly outside referrals.
> Two new fellows starting - more slots, slower notes. Expects the backlog to even out by spring.
> Nothing requested. Next visit end of Feb.

Jorge Maldonado, MD, Redwood Basin Medical Group, Sacramento, CA (RSM)
> Visit on January 27, approximately 20 minutes, in person at the Sacramento office.
> Discussion was limited to telehealth logistics: roughly one third of follow-up visits are now virtual, and the no-show rate for those slots was described as lower than for in-person appts.
> Two operational issues raised - patients cannot upload seizure diaries through the video platform, and interpreter scheduling requires 48 hours notice.
> No materials requested. Next contact expected mid-March.

Imani Okafor, MD, Smoky Ridge Medical Center, Knoxville, TN (RSM)
> Fourth conversation with this prescriber since September 2025; visit on February 3, approximately 25 minutes.
> Brought up post-stroke epilepsy again and said these patients do not fit neatly into any of the usual categories.
> Estimated six to eight such referrals over the past twelve months, most of them age 60 or older, and noted that the stroke service sends them over without a clear pathway back.
> No materials were requested and no product claims were made during the discussion.

Robert Enloe, MD, High Desert Neurology, Boise, ID (AR)
> Visit on February 4, approximately 15 minutes, at the Boise office.
> Topic was adminstrative burden only. Estimated that prior authorization paperwork consumes four to six hours of staff time per week across the practice, up from two to three hours in 2024.
> One staff member now handles appeals part time. Described the payer portals as inconsistent, with three different formats requested for the same information.
> No product specifics were discussed and nothing was requested.

Harold Jessup, MD, Magnolia Grove Clinic, Jackson, MS (AR)
> Visit on February 5, approximately 30 minutes; second discussion with this clinic in 2026.
> Called titration in geriatric patients 'a second job' for caregivers and asked for simpler guidance.
> Elaborated that most patients over 65 in the panel arrive on five or more concomitant medications, and that any schedule change generates a call from a family member.
> Estimated that two of every three older patients need a pharmacist review before a change is made, which adds about a week to the decision.
> Request logged: caregiver-facing education on what to expect during a titration period, at label level. Routing to Medical Information.

Yolanda Reyes, MD, Copper Mesa Neurology, Mesa, AZ (RSM)
> Brief encounter on January 29, under ten minutes, in the clinic corridor.
> Conversation was social: a two-week trip to Oaxaca over the holidays, and the usual observation that February in Mesa is the only compensation for July.
> Also asked about flight routing to Seoul for a family trip in the fall.
> No clinical or product discussion took place.

Mei-Lin Tsang, MD, Bayview Epilepsy Associates, Oakland, CA (RSM)
> Visit on February 6, approximately 20 minutes, at the Oakland site.
> Discussion stayed at the level of the general ASM landscape: counted eleven agents in routine use at the center, and observed that the number of mechanisms represented is smaller than the number of molecules.
> Noted that formulary review now runs twice a year rather than annually, and that the committee asks for class-level summaries rather than single-agent reviews.
> No efficacy or comparative claims were made by either party, and no materials were requested.

Fiona Gallagher, MD, Great Lakes Epilepsy Institute, Madison, WI (RSM)
> Quick stop at Great Lakes, ~15 min in the fellows room.
> Pt volume up again this quarter, mostly new referrals in from the western half of the state. Epilepsy service running two extra half-days to absorb it.
> Video EEG wait is the choke point, out around nine weeks. F/u slots get pushed first.
> No clinical questions, no materials requested. Next appt not booked.

Andrei Petrov, MD, Prairie Gate Health, Des Moines, IA (RSM)
> Longer than planned, ~30 min, mostly standing in the back hallway. Second visit to this site this yaer.
> Asked where the gaps sit in the refractory panel right now. Said the 12-to-17 group with refractory focal epilepsy is where the biggest gap sits, since the adult-only label leaves them waiting.
> Two pts in mind, both failed 2 ASMs, both still seizing. Says the practical plan is hold and re-book until they age in, and that parents hear the same answer every visit.
> I confirmed CNB is approved for adults only and did not discuss use under 18. No request to do so was made.
> Logging as recurring unmet need - same theme heard in Madison and Baton Rouge. No AE, nothing requested.

Katherine Ost, MD, Sonoran Neuroscience Institute, Tucson, AZ (RSM)
> ~20 min, in person, squeezed between clinic blocks.
> Whole convo was the EHR. Seizure frequency template takes one number per encounter, no feild for clusters, so the real count ends up buried in free text.
> Says the QI chart review meant opening every note by hand. Two tickets in the IT queue since Jan, no movement.
> No product discussion. Nothing requested.

Jorge Maldonado, MD, Redwood Basin Medical Group, Sacramento, CA (RSM)
> Drop-in, ~10 min, waiting room was full so we stood in the corridor.
> All admin. Says the front desk now loses about a day a week to payer forms, and the same clinical question comes back in three diffrent formats.
> Denials arrive by mail, appeals go through a portal, and nobody in the office can tell which one the payer actually reads.
> No product specifics came up and I did not raise any. No AE.

Alice Nguyen-Barr, MD, Old Dominion Neurology Group, Richmond, VA (AR)
> In person, ~15 min at the Richmond office. First contact since Feb.
> Telehealth f/u is about a quarter of the schedule now and staying that way. No-shows down, but the check-in link expires if a pt opens it early, so the front desk re-sends most mornings.
> Diaries still arrive on paper or by fax. Staff re-key them before the appt, which is where the time goes.
> No clinical or product discussion. Next appt not booked.

Mei-Lin Tsang, MD, Bayview Epilepsy Associates, Oakland, CA (RSM)
> The visit ran about twenty-five minutes and stayed almost entirely on staffing, which I gather has been the dominant topic at the center since the new year.
> Two of the four advanced practice providers left within the same quarter, and the replacement postings have been open since January without a strong candidate, so the epilepsy service is now covering intake with attending time that used to go to reading studies.
> The practical result, as it was described to me, is that new patient appointments are being booked eleven to twelve weeks out, and follow-up visits are the first thing to move whenever someone calls out sick.
> I was asked, politely, whether our team could plan visits around the academic calendar. I said I would be glad to work within whatever window the clinic prefers and would confirm before the next trip.
> No clinical or product topics were raised on either side, and nothing was requested.

Victor Salas, MD, Hill Country Neuroscience Institute, Austin, TX (RSM)
> A brief conversation, perhaps fifteen minutes, in the resident workroom while the afternoon list was being divided up.
> Teaching load has grown this year: four residents rotate through the epilepsy service rather than two, and the medical student clerkship now falls in the same spring block.
> Journal club has moved to Wednesday evenings, with the reading list chosen by the fellows themselves through June, an arrangement I was told works far better for attendance than the previous faculty-selected format.
> The one frustration mentioned was that fellowship interview season overlaps with the busiest clinic weeks, so applications end up being read on weekends.
> Nothing was requested and no clinical or product topics came up.

Yolanda Reyes, MD, Copper Mesa Neurology, Mesa, AZ (RSM)
> Roughly twenty minutes in the office at the end of the morning clinic; this was the third contact with this practice since the autumn.
> The discussion stayed general, on how crowded the antiseizure medication landscape has become. The observation offered was that a community neurologist now chooses among more agents than mechanisms, and that keeping the distinctions straight is its own small burden.
> Related to that, formulary tiering at the two dominant local plans was described as the practical constraint that shapes sequencing more than anything said at a meeting does.
> No efficacy or comparative claims were made by either party, and I offered none. Nothing was requested and I left no materials.

Fiona Gallagher, MD, Great Lakes Epilepsy Institute, Madison, WI (RSM)
> A short visit, about ten minutes, mostly to sort out plans for the regional epilepsy meeting in June.
> The institute is sending three attendings, two fellows and one nurse practitioner this year, one more than last year, and there was a question about whether the Saturday sessions run into the afternoon, since several of the group are flying home that evening.
> I was asked, politely, whether I would be attending, and I said that I expect to be and would be glad to say hello there rather than take up clinic time for it.
> Mentioned in passing that the registartion portal was rejecting institutional email addresses last week; the meeting office has apparently since fixed it.
> No clinical or product discussion, and nothing was requested.

Imani Okafor, MD, Smoky Ridge Medical Center, Knoxville, TN (RSM)
> Approximately twenty minutes in the clinic office; this was my first visit to the site this year.
> Patient volume was the whole topic. The quarter has run noticably heavier than the same period last year, and the increase is coming almost entirely from primary care referrals rather than from the hospital side.
> The practice added a Thursday evening clinic in February to absorb it, though I was told this has mostly relocated the backlog rather than reduced it, and that documentation now spills past dinner.
> No questions were raised for me, no materials were requested, and no product topics arose. I offered to keep the next visit short and was told that mid-summer would be easier.

Katherine Ost, MD, Sonoran Neuroscience Institute, Tucson, AZ (RSM)
> Meeting held on June 2 at the Tucson campus, approximately twenty minutes, at the clinic's request.
> The discussion concerned staffing only. One of the two nurse practitioners supporting the epilepsy clinic transferred to the inpatient service in April and recruitment has not yet closed; new patient scheduling has moved from six weeks to roughly ten.
> I was asked to keep future visits within a fixed monthly window so that they do not displace clinical slots, which I have agreed to do.
> Follow-ups: (1) propose two standing visit windows for the third quarter, (2) confirm with the office manager whether late afternoons remain preferable.

Jorge Maldonado, MD, Redwood Basin Medical Group, Sacramento, CA (RSM)
> Brief encounter on June 3, under ten minutes, in the clinic corridor between appts.
> The conversation was social: two weeks in Lisbon in May, and the observation that valley heat arrived a full month early this year, with the building air handling being blamed for the remainder.
> I was also asked for a recommendation on rail travel in Japan for a family trip in the autumn, which I could not provide with any authority.
> No clinical or product discussion took place, and nothing was requested.

Naomi Feldman, MD, Twin Rivers University Hospital, Columbus, OH (RSM)
> Meeting held on June 4 at Twin Rivers, approximately thirty-five minutes; third contact with this center since October 2025.
> The scheduled topic was the transition clinic, which now sees patients from age sixteen jointly with pediatric neurology twice a month.
> Raised, unprompted, that a 16-year-old with drug-resistant focal seizures had to stay on a failing regimen because cenobamate is not approved below 18.
> I confirmed that the XCOPRI indication in the United States is limited to adults and did not discuss use below that age; no request to do so was made. The point being made concerned the absence of an option and what is said to the family in the meantime.
> Follow-ups: (1) log as a recurring unmet need in the adolescent population, the fourth such account recorded this quarter, (2) ask Medical Information which published adolescent pharmacokinetic literature, if any, may be shared on request, (3) no safety event was described and nothing has been routed to safety.

Robert Enloe, MD, High Desert Neurology, Boise, ID (AR)
> Telephone conversation on June 5, approximately ten minutes, at my request.
> The practice is sending one physician and one MA to the regional epilepsy meeting this month, and asked whether the Friday sessions are listed in the main program or seperately.
> A second question concerned whether the poster session runs over the lunch hour, since the return flight is already booked for that evening.
> Follow-ups: (1) forward the published program once the meeting office releases it, (2) confirm the poster session hours. No clinical or product topics were discussed.

Priya Raghavan, MD, North Star Neurology, Minneapolis, MN (RSM)
> Visit on June 1, approximately fifteen minutes, held in a temporary office on the ground floor.
> The second floor is closed for mechanical work until September, so the neurology clinic is operating out of four borrowed rooms and one shared workstation.
> The substantive complaint was parking: the staff lot is now a construction laydown area, the replacement lot is a nine-minute walk, and patients arriving with a driver are being dropped at a service entrance that is not signed.
> Nothing was requested of me. I offered to defer the next visit until the clinic returns upstairs, and that was accepted.

Susan Ratliff, MD, Harborlight Neurology, Portland, ME (AR)
> Meeting held on June 5 by video, approximately twenty minutes.
> Roughly one third of follow-up visits at this practice are now virtual and the intention is to keep that share; the stated reason is that patients driving in from inland counties otherwise miss appts altogether.
> Two constraints were described precisely. First, a substantial minority of patients join by audio only, so nothing observable is gained over an ordinary telephone call. Second, several patients winter out of state, which raises a licensure question the practice has not resolved and which the billing service answers differently each time it is asked.
> Nothing was requested of me and no product topics were raised. I asked whether a video slot would be preferred for our own contacts and was told that in person remains easier, ideally late in the day.

Mei-Lin Tsang, MD, Bayview Epilepsy Associates, Oakland, CA (RSM)
> Short catch-up after grand rounds. Panel is mostly refractory adults, several followed for a decade plus.
> Volunteered that the longest-standing refractory patient in the panel has had the quietest quarter in years since starting cenobamate.
> Framed as one pt observation only. Said back that single cases dont generalize; logging it as individual experience, nothing more.
> Diary habits unchanged - paper first, then scanned into the chart by staff.
> Next touchpoint at dept mtg. 15 min slot, agenda already full.

Fiona Gallagher, MD, Great Lakes Epilepsy Institute, Madison, WI (RSM)
> Teaching talk only this visit. Runs journal club for the PGY3s every other Thurs, trying to move it to a lunch slot.
> Gripe: fellows rotate out mid-block so the critical appraisal series never finishes.
> Picked up two extra resident lectures this term. Prep time comes out of clinc admin time.
> Nothing clinical raised. Cut short, called away to an EEG read.

Yolanda Reyes, MD, Copper Mesa Neurology, Mesa, AZ (RSM)
> Front desk down two schedulers since Feb. New referrals sitting 6-7 wks.
> Triage is nurse-led for now. Follow-ups get bumped first, which the whole office dislikes.
> Asked that visits stay under 10 min until the roles are backfilled. Fine by me.
> No other topics. Fuller discussion pushed to next quarter.

Peter Kowalczyk, MD, Green Mountain Neuroscience, Burlington, VT (RSM)
> East wing is a construction zone thru summer. Clinic relocated to 2nd floor temporarily.
> Main gripe is parking - staff lot closed, shuttle runs late, pts arriving 20 min behind.
> Says drilling noise makes afternoon phone visits nearly impossible.
> No clinical topics. Will try again once the move settles.

Caleb Munson, MD, Cedar Ridge Medical Group, Springfield, IL (AR)
> A long conversation, most of it about how referrals from the two local pediatric practices reach this clinic well before those patients turn eighteen.
> Described the habit of 'parking' adolescent drug-resistant cases until 18, calling it an uncomfortable way to practice.
> To be precise about what was said, the framing was administrative rather than clinical - the prescriber follows these patients, keeps the existing regimen, and waits, because the approved population begins at adulthood.
> No use outside the approved population was discussed or implied at any point, and I said the observation would be recorded as field feedback for our medical team.
> We closed on scheduling; the earliest slot the practice can offer is late August.

Imani Okafor, MD, Smoky Ridge Medical Center, Knoxville, TN (RSM)
> Most of our time went to the new encounter template, which apparently forces a single seizure count per visit even when patients describe several event types.
> The workaround has been a free-text line at the bottom of the note, so the counts cannot be searched later, and that is the part that frustrates this clinic most.
> Two medical assistants are re-entering diaries by hand after clinic, and informatics has an open ticket that has not moved since spring.
> I offered nothing beyond sympathy, since this is an internal systems matter; I note it only because chart-based questions take noticeably longer at this site.

Jorge Maldonado, MD, Redwood Basin Medical Group, Sacramento, CA (RSM)
> This visit was almost entirely about telehealth logistics: roughly a third of follow-ups are now video, and the clinic is deciding which visit types should stay remote permanently.
> The practical complaint is bandwith at the patient end rather than the platform itself, so the front office has started calling patients the day before to test the link.
> Interstate licensing came up as well, since a number of patients drive in from Nevada and therefore cannot be seen remotely.
> There was no clinical discussion today; the physician was between video blocks and we spoke in the corridor for about ten minutes.

Katherine Ost, MD, Sonoran Neuroscience Institute, Tucson, AZ (RSM)
> The conversation was mostly about the regional epilepsy meeting in the fall - which sessions justify the travel, and whether the institute will send fellows this year.
> Two colleagues from the neurophysiology group have submitted abstracts, and the hope is that acceptance frees up travel funds for junior staff.
> I was asked whether our people would be in the exhibit area, and I confirmed only that colleagues usually attend and that I would forward the agenda once it is published.
> We agreed to compare calendars in September, since the meeting overlaps with the annual EEG course.

Priya Raghavan, MD, North Star Neurology, Minneapolis, MN (RSM)
> Nearly all of the time was spent on paperwork burden in general terms: prior authorization volume across the whole practice has roughly doubled in two years, by the office manager's count.
> One staff member now handles authorizations and appeals full time, and the physician described spending part of most evenings on peer-to-peer calls that could have been a form.
> No product or therapy specifics were raised, and I introduced none; the point being made was about administrative load, not about any particular treatment.
> The only request was that visits be scheduled around the Tuesday authorization block, which I have noted for future planning.

Robert Enloe, MD, High Desert Neurology, Boise, ID (AR)
> A brief and largely social visit. Smoke from the fires south of town had closed the trail network, and much of the conversation concerned a postponed rafting trip.
> August travel will leave the practice with one covering physician, so the schedule is deliberately light that month.
> I was asked, politely, whether I still drive the full loop across the state, and we compared notes on which mountain passes are worth avoiding in winter.
> Nothing clinical was raised and I introduced nothing; I will plan a substantive visit for September.

Yolanda Reyes, MD, Copper Mesa Neurology, Mesa, AZ (RSM)
> Visit on May 19. Discussion limited to volume: the clinic logged about 340 encounters in April against 290 in January, per the practice manager's dashbaord.
> Most of the increase is attributed to two referring internists who joined the network on March 2.
> New-patient slots are booked into the week of July 6; return visits are holding at three weeks.
> Neutral on whether the trend holds past the summer. No clinical or product topics were discussed.

Mei-Lin Tsang, MD, Bayview Epilepsy Associates, Oakland, CA (RSM)
> Visit on May 20, about 25 minutes. The conversation stayed at the level of the antiseizure landscape in general - the observation offered was that the number of available ASMs has roughly doubled since the early 2000s.
> The point was about choice architecture rather than any individual agent: formulary lists, teaching order, and how residents are taught to sequence options.
> No comparative or efficacy statement was made about any product, and I made none; I record the topic only because it frames how this center builds its internal pathways.
> Follow-up set for the week of June 15, at the request of the physician.

Walter Brandt, MD, Flint Hills Neuroscience, Wichita, KS (AR)
> Visit on May 21, 30 minutes, in office between afternoon appts.
> About 40% of the panel is 65 or older by the practice's own estimate, and most of those patients arrive on five or more concomitant medications.
> Triple-checks interactions before considering cenobamate in anyone over 65, which slows the decision down.
> Routine as described: pharmacist review first, then a second pass through the XCOPRI label section on interactions, then a decision at the next visit - usually two to three weeks later.
> Stated plainly that the hesitation is process time rather than any observed event; nothing was reported about a specific patient.

Fiona Gallagher, MD, Great Lakes Epilepsy Institute, Madison, WI (RSM)
